title: Avalokiteshvara looks deep
hookLine: the bodhisattva of compassion, practicing deep wisdom, sees the five heaps empty

lines: A THOUSAND ARMS, A WHITE ROBE.
cards: If you've ever seen a statue of a serene figure with a thousand arms, each hand holding out something different, or a graceful white-robed figure in a Chinese garden, or a small shrine in a Japanese hospital, you may have met the same being under different names.
In China she's often Guanyin. In Japan, Kannon. In Tibet, Chenrezig.
In India, where the name began, Avalokiteshvara. And the Heart Sutra opens by pointing straight at this figure. Today's word: Avalokiteshvara.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO HEARS THE WORLD'S CRIES.
teach.b: In the Mahayana, a bodhisattva is someone on the way to full awakening who vows to help all beings get there too. Avalokiteshvara is the bodhisattva of compassion, the one who hears the cries of the world.
The name is usually read as avalokita, looking down or looking upon, and ishvara, lord: the lord who looks down with compassion. In the art, the thousand arms are for reaching everyone who calls.
In Tibet, the Dalai Lamas are regarded as his emanations. In East Asia, over the centuries, the figure came to be shown most often as female. Here's the surprise in the Heart Sutra's first line.
It doesn't show Avalokiteshvara doing something compassionate. It shows the bodhisattva looking.

teach.h: LOOKING DEEP AT THE FIVE HEAPS.
teach.b: Practicing deep in the perfection of wisdom, the text says, Avalokiteshvara looked closely and saw five heaps, and saw that they were empty. Five heaps: you met them a week ago, the khandhas.
Form, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness. The Pali name was khandha; here, in Sanskrit, it's skandha. Same five.
What it means for them to be empty is where the sutra goes next, slowly, tomorrow. For today, notice the pairing. The being most well-known for compassion is the one who teaches wisdom.
In Mahayana teaching the two are often called the two wings of a bird: compassion without wisdom can't see clearly, and wisdom without compassion doesn't fly.
The sutra begins with both in one figure.

how: Devotion to Avalokiteshvara, as Guanyin, Kannon, Gwaneum or Chenrezig, is among the most widespread in Mahayana and Tibetan Buddhism; many practitioners chant the Heart Sutra, which opens with this bodhisattva, alongside mantras and prayers to Avalokiteshvara.

o: an ancient Indian king who built the first stupas
the first teacher who brought Buddhism to Tibet
the bodhisattva of compassion, the lord who looks down

games.q: match each name to where it's used.

s: the Heart Sutra opens with Avalokiteshvara doing a compassionate deed
it opens with the bodhisattva looking deeply and seeing the five heaps empty.
the skandhas in the Heart Sutra are the same five heaps as the Pali khandhas
in East Asia the figure is often shown as female
over the centuries Guanyin came to be shown most often as female.

games.q: the bodhisattva of compassion appears at the start of a text on wisdom. what is Avalokiteshvara doing in the first line?
o: looking deeply, and seeing the five heaps empty.
games.why: the sutra begins with deep looking. in Mahayana teaching, compassion and wisdom are two wings of one bird.

practice: Choose one thing near you, your own hand, a leaf, a pen, and look at it deeply, the way Avalokiteshvara looks: not a quick glance, but staying with it, as if you'd never seen one before.
Notice its color, its edges, its texture, then the feeling tone it brings, pleasant, unpleasant or neither, and the label your mind puts on it. Then close your eyes and rest.

wordCard.voice: Avalokiteshvara. The bodhisattva of compassion, the lord who looks down, who in the Heart Sutra looks deep and sees the five heaps empty.

orig.note: Sanskrit avalokiteśvara: the lord who looks down, the bodhisattva of compassion.

carryVoice: Your line: look deep. The one who hears the world's cries begins by looking. Day two hundred sixty-eight.
